newsitem.title: UK: MOTOR RACING-DIGITAL TV DRIVES FORMULA ONE FLOTATION.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-DIGITAL TV DRIVES FORMULA ONE FLOTATION.

text.p: Formula One, revving up on Monday for a flotation that could value the glamour end of motor racing at $4 billion, is the latest sport aiming to cash in on the potential riches from pay-per-view television.
U.S. investment bank Salomon Brothers has confirmed it is talking to Briton Bernie Ecclestone, the business brain behind the sport, about a possible flotation.
Newspaper reports said the flotation, which could turn former second-hand car salesman Ecclestone into a billionaire, would involve listings in London and New York.

The $4 billion valuation is based largely on the potential income from media rights, in particular pay-per-view services which can be developed thanks to the extra channel capacity offered by digital television.

The 16 Grand Prix races a year command a worldwide television audience of 330 million viewers in some 130 countries. That could bring in annual revenue from global pay-per-view television coverage of one billion dollars within five years, London's Financial Times reported.

"Ecclestone has invested a large amount of money on digital television technology and is looking at making the viewer much more pro-active," said David Wilkinson, share analyst with London stockbroker Greig Middleton.
A vision of this future is offered by Germany's DF1 digital television service, launched last July to coincide with the German Grand Prix at Hockenheim.
DF1, owned by media magnate Leo Kirch, allows viewers to flick between images from the cockpit of top racers and shots and various cameras around the track.

Optimism about potential pay-per-view income fuelled a huge rise in the value of stock-market listed British soccer clubs last year. However, the sector has lost some 30 percent in value this year as investors have taken a more sober look at prospects.
Public appetite for pay-per-view sport is yet to be proven. DF1 in Germany has only an estimated 20,000 subscribers, while take-up for pay-per-view soccer in Italy has been disappointing.

"What is not clear is what the buy-rate for pay-per-view Formula One will be...It could be that viewers will think it is really good a few times but then not do it again," said Chris Renaud, an analyst at CSFB.
He said that investors could be interested in the flotation as means of buying into a content provider at a time when the number of television channels is multiplying.
But he said it was difficult to tell at this stage whether the widely reported $4 billion value was realistic.
"It is hard to put a valuation on the business. The devil really is in the detail."

Lawyers are believed to be at work on redrafting the complex network of contracts between Ecclestone's Formula One companies, the leading teams such as Williams, and the track owners in preparation for a possible flotation in July or August.
Ecclestone is reported to see a New York listing as a way to improve the sport's profile in the United States, one of the few countries where it has failed to take off.
The race calendar takes in South America and Canada but the Formula One circus does not go to any U.S. towns.
